smells.description: Circular dependency among 6 components: Default <-> Format <-> Jam <-> Jinfer <-> Jota <-> Toknroll
smells.explanation: Dependency cycles make components tightly coupled — you cannot change, test, or deploy any component in the cycle independently. This hinders maintainability, increases build times, and makes the system harder to understand.
smells.suggestion: Break the cycle by introducing an interface/abstraction that one component depends on, inverting the dependency direction. Consider the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP).

smells.description: Json contains 22 entities but only 0 internal dependencies (0.00 per entity), suggesting multiple responsibilities.
smells.explanation: Large components are harder to understand, test, and maintain. When their internals are also sparsely connected, that usually means the component is acting as a bucket for unrelated concerns rather than a cohesive module.
smells.suggestion: Consider splitting Json into smaller, focused components with single responsibilities.

smells.description: 'Config' pattern is scattered across 3 components: Default, Format, Jota
smells.explanation: When a single concern is spread across many components, changes to that concern require modifying multiple places, increasing the risk of inconsistencies and bugs.
smells.suggestion: Centralize 'Config'-related functionality into a dedicated component to reduce scattering.

smells.description: Format is depended on by 4 other components (67% of all components).
smells.explanation: A component with too many dependents becomes a bottleneck. Any change to it can cascade across the entire system, making evolution risky and expensive.
smells.suggestion: Consider splitting Format into smaller interfaces so dependents only couple to what they actually use (ISP).
